outcome: Nothing found since 26 January 2024 settles, or moves a quantity named in, the question whether there are infinitely many Giuga numbers; as of 11 October 2026 it is still open. The 2026 items are characterisations of Giuga numbers (López; Svinin), a computer certificate for a sequence the record does not define (Sorini and Guerra), a mailing-list primality test (Rotondo), and formal-conjectures issues; none addresses infinitude. The most recent bound on counterexamples to the neighbouring primality conjecture dates from 2013.
problem_asks: One question: are there infinitely many Giuga numbers? A Giuga number is a composite n such that every prime p dividing n also divides n/p - 1 (equivalently p² divides n - p for every such p). Parts asked: (1) whether the set of Giuga numbers is infinite. The statement does not ask whether any Giuga number is odd, whether a Giuga number can also be Carmichael, or whether Giuga's primality conjecture holds. Those are neighbouring questions and are recorded below as such.

events.what_happened: Miguel Ángel López (single author), arXiv:2610.09129 [math.NT], 'Idempotence in Carmichael and Giuga numbers and its application to the Agoh-Giuga conjecture'. Gives an arithmetic-function characterisation of composite Giuga numbers (Corollary 4.1: a composite n is Giuga iff a divisor sum of φ(d)(n/d)^φ(n) is congruent to -1 mod n), a prime-idempotent characterisation (Theorem 5.3), and an idempotence-based necessary condition for any Agoh-Giuga counterexample, which the author says presumably no number will satisfy. Does not address whether Giuga numbers are infinite.
events.revisions: v1 only, 6 Oct 2026, per the arXiv abstract page.
events.delivers: New characterisations of composite Giuga numbers (divisor-sum form; prime-idempotent form) and a reformulation of the Agoh-Giuga conjecture in idempotent terms. The author works mostly under the assumption that n is squarefree. None of this bears on whether the set of Giuga numbers is infinite.
events.remains: All of problem_asks: the infinitude of Giuga numbers. The Agoh-Giuga conjecture itself is not settled; the paper reformulates it.
events.directly_checkable: The divisor-sum test of Corollary 4.1 can be checked by hand or by computer on any composite n. I did not carry out that check.
events.direction: Neutral on infinitude. The author expects no Agoh-Giuga counterexample, which is consistent with the Agoh-Giuga conjecture but does not prove it.

events.what_happened: Andrei K. Svinin, 'On a certain arithmetic function defined via Bernoulli numbers', arXiv:2607.18607 [math.NT]. Defines χ(n) for odd n ≥ 3. The main theorem states that χ(n) is integer-valued exactly when n is a prime or an odd Giuga number. The paper says 'the existence of an odd Giuga number is equivalent to the negation of the Agoh-Giuga conjecture', and that 'the question of the existence of odd Giuga numbers is open'. Also links primes with χ(p)=p-1 to Novák-Carmichael numbers (OEIS A337119). The first version was submitted 21 Jul 2026 (per the Pith review page); the arXiv HTML shows v2 dated 5 Oct 2026.
events.revisions: v2 dated 5 Oct 2026 (arXiv HTML). v1 date taken from the Pith review page; I did not view the arXiv v1 listing.
events.delivers: A characterisation of the odd integers at which χ is integral (odd primes and odd Giuga numbers, per the author's main theorem; I did not verify the proof). It produces no new Giuga number and says nothing about whether there are infinitely many.
events.remains: The infinitude of Giuga numbers. The existence of odd Giuga numbers, which the paper itself treats as open.

checked_by.qualification: None. It is an automated model answering a fixed list of questions about the paper.
checked_by.what_they_did: Read the paper on 1 Aug 2026. Verdict: 'A new and mostly correct elementary reformulation of Agoh–Giuga, with one real but easily fixable gap in Lemma 1.3.' Flagged the sentence 'It can be proven that any odd Giuga number (if it exists) is a Carmichael number' as asserted without proof or reference.

events.time_since_posted: about 12 weeks as of 11 Oct 2026; no human engagement found
events.doubts: The automated referee's objections are the specific reasons for doubt. (1) The introduction asserts without proof that any odd Giuga number is Carmichael; the referee says the implication is true but unjustified. (2) A real gap in Lemma 1.3. No human reviewer found. I did not verify either point.
events.direction: Characterises a Bernoulli-defined function by primes and odd Giuga numbers. It ties the existence of odd Giuga numbers to the Agoh-Giuga conjecture. It does not prove or refute anything about infinitude.

events.what_happened: Laerte Sorini (University of Urbino) and Maria Letizia Guerra (University of Bologna), Zenodo record 22047714, 'Computational Certificate for i27692 = 8134 in Giuga's Rank Sequence', v1.0.0 (CC BY 4.0). Described as 'supplementary computational material for the exact computer-assisted proof of i27692=8134 in Giuga's rank sequence'. Ships an endpoint witness, exact certificate data, verification programs (Python and C++) and checksums. The companion manuscript, 'Giuga's Conjecture: Rank-Sequence Computation, Rigorous Branch-and-Bound Certification, and Extended Computational Data' (2026), was not located as a published or posted paper. Keywords include 'Giuga's conjecture', 'Carmichael numbers' and 'primality criteria'. The record does not define i_n or the rank sequence.
events.delivers: Unclear from the record. It states an exact certificate that a particular endpoint of 'Giuga's rank sequence' has rank 8134 at index 27692. Because the record does not define the sequence, I cannot say whether it concerns Giuga numbers as the problem defines them. Nothing in the record concerns whether the set of Giuga numbers is infinite.

events.what_happened: Davide Rotondo, SeqFan mailing list post 'A New Discovery on Prime Numbers: A Test Based on Giuga Numbers' (10 Sep 2026). Defines G(n) = sum of j^n for j from 1 to n, and T(n,k) = G(n)/(G(k)G(n-k)). Claims that for every prime n other than 2, the reduced numerators are divisible by n, verified to n = 672. Says n = 9 is the only composite that passes. Replies: Geoffrey Caveney (11 Sep 2026) noted that the definition differs from the standard Giuga condition and that odd composites above 9 fail (n = 15 fails for k = 3). Rotondo conceded the explanation had been unclear.
events.delivers: An empirical observation for primes up to 672, using a non-standard G(n) with exponent n rather than n-1. No proof. The author states only the primes-pass direction, so it is not a primality test. It does not concern the infinitude of Giuga numbers.

checked_by.qualification: Mailing-list participant. Not a verification of any proof, since none was offered.
checked_by.what_they_did: Pointed out that the definition differs from the standard Giuga number definition and that odd composites above 9 fail (n = 15 fails for k = 3). Noted that computing the sums to 672 is a contribution in itself.

events.directly_checkable: The numerical claim for small n can be checked by hand from the worked n = 5 example in the thread.
events.doubts: The author's own statement is one-directional (primes pass; composites not addressed). The G(n) used is not Giuga's. The author conceded the first explanation was unclear. The check stops at 672.
events.direction: Says nothing about the existence of infinitely many Giuga numbers. The 'Giuga numbers' in the title is a loose label for a different sum.

events.what_happened: Jonathan Borwein, Christopher Maitland and Matthew Skerritt, 'Computation of an Improved Lower Bound to Giuga's Primality Conjecture', INTEGERS 13 (2013), article A67. Per secondary summaries, any counterexample to Giuga's 1950 primality conjecture has at least 19,908 decimal digits, equivalently any number that is both Giuga and Carmichael. The bound uses structural properties of Giuga and Carmichael numbers rather than exhaustive search. Secondary sources also report 'at least 4771 prime factors, odd, square-free, and above 10^19907' attributed to Borwein, Skerritt and Maitland. A 2013 CARMA seminar abstract by Skerritt gives 19,907 digits.
events.delivers: A lower bound on the size of any counterexample to Giuga's primality conjecture: at least 19,908 digits (a Giuga-and-Carmichael number). This bounds a subclass of Giuga numbers and concerns the primality question, not the infinitude of Giuga numbers. Restriction: it says nothing about whether Giuga numbers exist in infinitely many cases.
events.remains: All of problem_asks. The primality conjecture itself is still open.

checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper. Referee process not verified.

events.doubts: Secondary sources disagree on the figures: 19,908 digits (INTEGERS, per summaries), 19,907 (2013 seminar abstract), and 4771 prime factors / 10^19907 (reported as this paper's result). The 4771 figure is attributed to arXiv 1305.1867 by a search summary, but that paper's abstract does not contain it, and I could not read its full text. The INTEGERS PDF itself was not retrieved (HTTP 503, then unreadable).
events.direction: Cuts against small counterexamples to the primality conjecture. Not toward or away from infinitude of Giuga numbers.

Whether this is the same Sorini as the 2026 authors is not established.

events.what_happened: Florian Luca, Carl Pomerance and Igor Shparlinski, 'On Giuga numbers', International Journal of Modern Mathematics. The counting function of Giuga numbers up to x is o(x^(1/2)) (abstract, per summaries), improving Tipu. Later papers cite it as O(x^(1/2)/(log x)²). Publication year varies across my sources (2007, 2008, 2009).
events.delivers: An upper bound on how many Giuga numbers are at most x. This is a statement about the counting function, which the problem does not ask. It does not show that the set is infinite, and an upper bound of this kind is consistent with infinitely many.

disputes.summary: Sorini (2001), as reported by Wikipedia's Agoh–Giuga article: a counterexample to Giuga's primality conjecture must exceed 10^36067. Borwein, Maitland and Skerritt (2013), per secondary summaries: at least 19,908 digits, with the same paper's bound cited as the best. Both bound the same quantity, so they cannot both be the best known bound. The 2001 source was not found, so this is unresolved rather than settled.

Smallest odd Giuga number: at least 9 prime factors (MathWorld, per search summary) versus at least 14 prime factors (Wikipedia Giuga article; Grau and Oller-Marcén per summary). Separately, a figure of at least 4771 prime factors for any counterexample to the primality conjecture (reported for Borwein, Skerritt and Maitland) concerns a different quantity. These are not reconciled in the sources I read.

Borwein et al. (1996) counterexample bound: 13,800 digits (Wikipedia; Open Problem Garden gives no bound) versus 13,887 digits (3459 distinct primes, per search summaries of the Monthly paper and of arXiv 1311.3522).

The 4771-prime-factor / 10^19907 result is attributed to Borwein, Skerritt and Maitland in a secondary search summary of arXiv 1305.1867. The abstract of that paper does not contain it, and the full text was unreadable to me. Unverified.

Known Giuga numbers: Wikipedia says thirteen are known and the list is complete to the 12th term; the OEIS A007850 data lists 12 terms and a note mentions a Giuga number with 10 prime factors that 'may not be the next term'.

summary: I ran 37 searches covering the problem's name and variants, the Giuga–Agoh primality conjecture and its bounds, the Carmichael and Lehmer neighbours, 2026 preprint and Zenodo activity, the formal-conjectures repository, OEIS, Wikipedia, and AI-specific queries (Wikipedia's AI-discoveries list, Erdős-AI coverage, AI referees, Lean). Nothing found since 26 January 2024 settles, or moves a quantity named in, the question whether the set of Giuga numbers is infinite; it remains open as of 11 October 2026. The window items are: López (arXiv:2610.09129, 6 Oct 2026), a single-author characterisation of Giuga numbers via idempotents, with a reformulation of Agoh–Giuga; Svinin (arXiv:2607.18607, submitted 21 Jul 2026), characterising integrality of χ(n) by primes and odd Giuga numbers, with an automated AI referee flagging one unproven sentence and a gap in Lemma 1.3; Sorini and Guerra (Zenodo, 21 Aug 2026), a computer certificate for index 27692 in 'Giuga's rank sequence', which the record does not define; Rotondo (SeqFan, 10 Sep 2026), a primes-only pattern checked to 672 with a non-standard G(n), corrected by a respondent; and formal-conjectures issues #2247 (Feb 2026, closed June as a duplicate) and #7040 (Oct 2026). Neighbouring window items: Bhattacharjee et al. (Zenodo, 1 Oct 2026) on Lehmer's problem, and a January 2026 Lehmer preprint reported withdrawn (unverified, Preprints.org returned 403). Older events are recorded above: the 1996 and 2013 bounds on counterexamples to the primality conjecture, the Grau–Oller-Marcén characterisations (2011), Luca–Pomerance–Shparlinski's counting bound (year disputed), Machacek on prime-power Giuga numbers, Sauvaget's retracted 2011 proof, and Schneider's 2006 search. Close calls: (a) whether the Svinin and López papers move the problem — they characterise Giuga numbers and reformulate Agoh–Giuga, but neither bears on infinitude, so I record them as no movement; (b) whether the Sorini–Guerra certificate concerns Giuga numbers — its sequence is undefined in the record, so its scope is unknown; (c) Sorini 2001's 10^36067 bound is known only through Wikipedia and conflicts with the 2013 figure's status as best. AI: no source I read credits an AI system with any of the mathematics on this problem. The only AI-linked item on the problem is formal-conjectures issue #2247, which says it 'was generated by an AI agent and reviewed by me' (the agent is unnamed; it produced the question statement, not mathematics), so none_found is false there. The Lehmer Zenodo record lists 'Claude (Anthropic)' as a contributor on a neighbouring problem without saying what it did, so systems is empty there too. Wikipedia's AI-discoveries list, checked through October 2026, has no Giuga or Carmichael entry. I also corrected a secondary-source error: one search summary said every Giuga number is Carmichael, which fails for 30 (not Carmichael).
competing_reading: The strongest case for reading 2026 as movement: López's characterisations and Svinin's equivalence (odd Giuga existence iff Agoh–Giuga fails) are the first substantive 2026 mathematics on Giuga numbers, and together they could be argued to push the problem toward resolution. The reply is that neither makes the set of Giuga numbers more or less infinite; both characterise or reformulate. A second reading: the Sorini–Guerra certificate might be a finite computational step toward structure that matters for infinitude if 'Giuga's rank sequence' is a Giuga-type object. That is possible but unestablished, because the record does not define the sequence, and a finite certificate still does not decide an infinite question.
what_would_settle_it: (1) The INTEGERS 2013 article (n67) and the 1996 Monthly paper, to fix the bounds and their wording on infinitude. (2) The source of Sorini's 2001 10^36067 claim. (3) The Sorini–Guerra companion manuscript, to define i_n and the rank sequence and say whether it concerns Giuga numbers. (4) The arXiv v1 listing and any referee reports for 2607.18607, and a readable PDF of 2610.09129 to check acknowledgements verbatim. (5) The Lean history of AgohGiuga.lean for any change in status. (6) An arXiv math.NT listing search for 'Giuga' filtered to 2024 onward, to confirm no unseen item.

judgement.why: The statement asks only whether the set of Giuga numbers is infinite. No event, before or after the snapshot, bears on that: the 2026 items are characterisations (López, Svinin) or formal-conjecture issues (scope none), a non-standard mailing-list pattern and Lehmer-problem work (variant), and an undefined finite certificate (none). The pre-snapshot primality-conjecture bounds concern a different question (counterexamples to Giuga's primality conjecture, i.e. Giuga-and-Carmichael numbers), so they are variant; Schneider's search is instances. The close call was Luca–Pomerance–Shparlinski's o(x^(1/2)) counting bound: an upper bound on the counting function is consistent with infinitude and does not move any quantity the statement names, so none rather than bound. No event credits an AI with mathematics; issue #2247's AI agent only drafted the question statement, and the Lehmer Zenodo 'Claude' contributor role is unstated and on a different problem.
judgement.doubts: The Sorini–Guerra 'rank sequence' is undefined in the record; if it turned out to concern Giuga numbers directly it would still be a finite certificate. Several pre-snapshot figures rest on secondary summaries.
